question: Rephrase a passage where you state a character's emotion outright, and instead hint at the feeling through external cues the narrator observes.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: This style of minimally displayed emotion relies on external cues—what the narrator observes, for instance—to hint at what characters are feeling without coming right out and saying it.

question: Insert summary even outside natural lulls where a scene needs clarification or a fuller sense of a character's history, motivation, or emotion—a natural point of entry is still better.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: They can occur (within reason) anywhere that the scene needs clarification or will benefit from our more fully understanding characters' histories, motivations, or emotions. But, if you can find a natural point of entry for your summary, all the better.

question: After rendering a dramatic event in scene, transition back into summary so the event reads as part of the ongoing, ordinary reality rather than an isolated shock.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Fittingly, right after the scene of the death, O'Brien returns to his litany of the things they carried.

question: Pace a scene's interruptions to mirror the character's state of mind—for a drowsy character, break the foreground action with fragments that recreate in-and-out-of-consciousness.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: But the movement of the scene is intended to recreate the in-and-out-ofconsciousness experience of someone struggling, not very successfully, to stay awake.
